title: Peer binary hashing reads the entire executable into memory
description:
persona-grpc/src/consumer_attest.rs:72-76 — hash_file() does `std::fs::read(path)` to load the whole binary, then hashes it:

    let data = std::fs::read(path)?;
    Ok(Sha256::digest(&data).into())

What goes wrong: the peer binary is arbitrary — a browser or Electron app is 100-300MB. This allocates a buffer the full size of the peer's executable just to stream it through SHA-256. It is also a synchronous, unbounded-size read: attest_peer() is a sync fn (consumer_attest.rs:16) intended to be called from the tonic connection path, so that read blocks a tokio worker thread for the duration.

Fix, no new dependency and fewer lines of intermediate state: open the file and `std::io::copy` it into the hasher (sha2::Sha256 implements std::io::Write), which streams in fixed-size chunks with no full-file buffer. If it stays on an async path, wrap the call in tokio::task::spawn_blocking.

Note attest_peer() is currently not called from anywhere (see the dead-surface issue), so this is cheap to fix before it is wired in.
